clue.text: Wind from the east Portuguese region wiping out half of five hundred, say, in city centre

indicators.note: in an across clue, from the east means read from right to left, backwards

parts.note: fart is slang for breaking wind

indicators.note: wiping out means erasing, so letters are taken away from the region

parts.note: the Algarve is the southern coastal region of Portugal

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word is two of its letters, here the second pair

parts.note: its second half gives VE
one hundred is ten times ten, a square number, so it exemplifies a square

explanation.surface: A traveller's complaint about wind, Portugal and an odd sum in a city centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the east' means read right to left in an across answer; 'half of five' is the back half of the word five, which 'wiping out' takes from the Algarve. One hundred is ten squared, hence 'say'. Trafalgar Square is London's central plaza.
explanation.definitionFit: Trafalgar Square is the large public plaza at the heart of London, often treated as its central point.

clue.text: With added height, being short, this artist would represent three cities

indicators.note: The height is added to the answer to reach the cities, so the answer itself must be those letters short.
The painter was famously short in the leg, and the letters are short too — they stop before the third city is complete.

parts.note: The first is the pink-brick city on the Garonne in southern France.
The second is Los Angeles, which everybody shortens to its two initials.
The third is Utrecht in the Netherlands, arriving without its last two letters.
HT is the standard abbreviation for height, and those are the two letters the cities have and the wordplay does not.

explanation.surface: A painter who, given a few more inches, would somehow stand for three cities instead of one man.
explanation.walkthrough: Toulouse-Lautrec's legs stopped growing when he was a teenager, so 'being short' is a joke about the man before it is an instruction about letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec is the Montmartre painter of the Moulin Rouge posters, so 'this artist' points at one particular man.

clue.text: Surprisingly AC Milan dropping name for club initially gets praise

indicators.note: surprisingly hints at something unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order
dropping means letting go, so one letter is lost from the club name
for means in place of, so a new letter stands where the old one was

parts.note: the Italian football club, taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, picking the first letter

parts.note: supplies its first letter C

explanation.surface: AC Milan surprisingly lose a big name, yet the club's early form wins praise.
explanation.walkthrough: In AC MILAN, C (club 'initially') replaces N ('dropping name for'), giving ACMILAC; 'Surprisingly' rearranges those letters. AC Milan is an Italian football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim is enthusiastic public approval, so it is a strong form of praise.

clue.text: A drapery that's hard to break is falling down?

definitions.note: The setter defines by describing what the thing does rather than naming it, so a participle phrase stands in for a noun; the question mark owns the stretch.

parts.note: The opening word is taken at face value as the single letter it is.

indicators.note: Breaking into a place means getting inside it, so the letter beside it forces its way in.

parts.note: A valance is the strip of drapery hung round a bed frame or along a curtain rail.
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard, and it is what breaks in near the end.

explanation.surface: A curtain too tough to tear, apparently on the point of coming down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to break' reads as one phrase about tough fabric; the setter splits it, so 'hard' is a letter and 'to break' is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An avalanche is a mass of snow falling down a mountainside, so the phrase names the event by describing it.

clue.text: A dose of Farage no alternative for the City

indicators.note: A dose is a measured portion taken out of something larger, here a run of letters lifted from the middle.

parts.note: Five letters run straight on across these three words, starting four letters into the first.

explanation.surface: A dose of Nigel Farage prescribed to the Square Mile, with nothing else on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The City' with its capital letter is London's financial district on the surface; the setter means an Italian port instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Genoa is a big Italian port, so 'the City' defines it by example — any city fits, and this one is buried in the clue.

clue.text: People like Trump and Putin lacking leadership for members of the local community

indicators.note: lacking leadership means without the leading letter, so the first letter goes

parts.note: Trump and Putin are both presidents

explanation.surface: Trump and Putin lack leadership, unlike the people next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking leadership' drops the leading P of PRESIDENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents are the people who live in a place, so they make up its local population.

clue.text: Unconventional rock band dismissive of new record's opening

indicators.note: Being dismissive of something is brushing it aside, and what gets brushed aside here is N, the usual abbreviation for new.

parts.note: The rock band is Freddie Mercury's, and it turns up minus the letter that has been brushed aside.

indicators.note: An opening is the very start of a thing, so only the first letter of the word before it is taken.

parts.note: The first letter of 'record' is tacked on at the end.

explanation.surface: A rock band turning up its nose at the first track on a new record.
explanation.walkthrough: The band's name has to be spotted before anything can be taken off it, and 'new' turns out to be a letter rather than an adjective describing the record.
explanation.definitionFit: Queer's older sense is odd, off the usual pattern, which is exactly what 'unconventional' asks for.

clue.text: Symptom of a cold caught an hour after noon — go away!

parts.note: The hour after noon is one o'clock — 'at 1', with the 1 written as the Roman numeral.
Shoo is what you say to send a cat or a pigeon off.

explanation.surface: Somebody catches a cold at one in the afternoon and is told in no uncertain terms to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: Clock time is written straight into the letters: 'at one' becomes AT plus a Roman numeral, a numeral-for-number swap worth expecting whenever a clue names an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Atishoo is the comic-strip spelling of a sneeze, the symptom you get once a cold has been caught.

clue.text: Exciting comprehensive that won't leave you cold

parts.note: An electric atmosphere is an exciting one, charged and alive.
A blanket ban covers everything without exception, which is what comprehensive means.

explanation.surface: A thrilling non-selective secondary school, the sort that takes all comers.
explanation.walkthrough: A comprehensive is Britain's non-selective state secondary, which is the school the surface conjures up; the setter wants the adjective sense instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave someone cold is to fail to excite them, and this thing does the opposite twice over: it warms the bed and it thrills.

clue.text: Loveless workers' association introducing tea for free

indicators.note: Love is the tennis word for a nought, so something loveless has lost its O.
Introducing one thing to another puts it in among them, so the short word lands inside the long one.

parts.note: A workers' association is a UNION, here with its O gone and a gap left in the middle.
Cha is tea, a word English took from Chinese and kept in 'a nice cup of cha'.

explanation.surface: A trade union without a shred of affection in it, handing out free tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loveless' reads as a description of a hard-hearted union and is really an instruction to drop a letter. Love for nought comes from tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: To unchain something is to release it from its fetters, which is 'free' in its plainest verb sense.

clue.text: Tireless criminal abandons a son for being unproductive

indicators.note: criminal in the sense of crooked, so the letters are bent into a new order
abandons means leaves behind, so these letters are removed from the pool

parts.note: the word, taken as written for rearranging
S is the abbreviation for son, and a means one of them

explanation.surface: A tireless criminal walks out on his son and proves unproductive.
explanation.walkthrough: TIRELESS has one S more than the answer: when it 'abandons a son' it leaves TIRELES, and 'criminal' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile means barren or incapable of producing offspring or results, so it is fruitless.

clue.text: After retirement I see a way of working in US city

indicators.note: Retiring is going back the way you came, so the assembled letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: 'Ah!' is the noise you make when the penny drops.
The article is taken as the single letter it is.
A criminal's MO is their modus operandi, their way of working.

explanation.surface: A pensioner explaining that they have finally grasped how the job gets done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' is not a claim about eyesight but the noise of understanding, and the surface's talk of retirement is the only word doing mechanical work.
explanation.definitionFit: Omaha is the biggest city in Nebraska, so 'US city' defines it by example rather than by anything peculiar to it.

clue.text: Try to follow lunar astronaut circling earth who's missing in Hampshire town

indicators.note: What follows comes after, so the piece clued first ends up at the back of the answer.
Circling something means going round it, so one group of letters closes round a single one.

parts.note: Buzz Aldrin was the second man on the Moon; his surname turns up without the letters the clue says are missing.
E is the electrician's abbreviation for earth, the wire that runs to the ground.

indicators.note: The pronoun points back at the astronaut, and what he is missing is the two letters named next.

parts.note: These are the two letters the astronaut's name is missing.
A shot at something is a try at it, as in 'give it a shot'.

explanation.surface: An astronaut in lunar orbit circling the Earth, with somebody unaccounted for down below.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'in' does double duty: it reads as part of 'missing in Hampshire' and is really the pair of letters taken out of the astronaut's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldershot is the Hampshire garrison town that calls itself the home of the British Army.

clue.text: House dependency, conservatory, in the end leaves a mark

indicators.note: 'In the end' points at the final letter of the word beside it rather than at the word itself.
To leave is to depart, so the letter just identified walks out of the second piece.

parts.note: A semi is Britain's semi-detached house, one of a pair sharing a wall.
A dependency is a COLONY, a territory run from elsewhere, and it turns up a letter short.
The last letter of 'conservatory' is the one that departs.

explanation.surface: An estate agent listing a house, its granny flat and finally its conservatory.
explanation.walkthrough: COLONY and 'conservatory' end in the same letter, which is what lets one word name the letter another has to lose.
explanation.definitionFit: A semicolon is a punctuation mark, so 'a mark' names the family it belongs to rather than the thing itself.

clue.text: Working title of film oddly omitted recurring theme

indicators.note: A word being worked is a word being put through a process, and the process here rearranges its letters.

parts.note: These seven letters go into the mix exactly as they stand.

indicators.note: The odd-numbered letters are the ones left out, so only the even ones survive.

parts.note: Take out the first and third letters of 'film' and IM is what is left.

explanation.surface: A film's working title being quietly dropped, and a theme that keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working title' is a real phrase about films, which is why it takes a while to see 'Working' pulling away from it to do a job of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A leitmotif is the short musical phrase Wagner attached to a character and brought back each time, so a theme that recurs.

clue.text: Sign Keir's opponent is losing her head when drinking orange juice

indicators.note: A head is the top or front of a thing, so the name loses its first letter.
Someone drinking takes the liquid inside them, so those letters go within.

parts.note: Keir Starmer's opposite number across the despatch box is Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and her first name goes headless.
OJ is the breakfast-menu shorthand for orange juice.

explanation.surface: The leader of the opposition losing her composure over a glass of breakfast juice.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain's two main party leaders face each other weekly at Prime Minister's Questions, so 'Keir's opponent' is a particular person rather than a general one.
explanation.definitionFit: An emoji is a little picture standing for a feeling or a thing, which is a sign in the plain sense of a symbol.

clue.text: Position in church Liz mostly combined with shepherd after second husband left

indicators.note: combined means mixed together, so all these letters are blended into a new order
mostly means not quite all, so the name loses its last letter

parts.note: the name, trimmed to LI

indicators.note: after second points to the second of the word's two husband letters
left means departed, so the letter is taken out

parts.note: the word, taken as written

explanation.surface: A church role goes to Liz, joined with a shepherd after her second husband walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims LIZ to LI; removing the second H of SHEPHERD ('second husband left') leaves SHEPERD; 'combined' mixes the two. 'shepherd' suggests the church sense of a pastor, but here it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Eldership is the office of an elder, a lay leadership role in Presbyterian and other churches.

clue.text: Wrongly ordered energy drinks, a mistake

indicators.note: Something wrongly ordered has its parts in the wrong sequence, so the letters need putting back into the right one.

parts.note: E is physics' symbol for energy, as in Einstein's equation.
A cat laps its milk, so a word for drinking hands over four letters.

explanation.surface: Somebody has put in the wrong order for the energy drinks, which is a slip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy drinks' reads as one thing off a supermarket shelf; the setter uses the two words separately, and 'drinks' is the verb, not the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or small failure of attention, so 'a mistake' is the everyday synonym.

clue.text: One organises nationals in real power going to heaven

definitions.note: 'One organises' is the crossword's way of writing 'one who organises': the relative pronoun is left out, so the phrase names a person rather than an action.

indicators.note: 'In' is the plainest container instruction there is: what precedes it goes inside what follows.
Heaven is up, and in a down clue up means from the bottom of the entry towards the top, so the letters are read the other way.

parts.note: The word goes in whole, with the pair of Ns pushed into the middle of it.
Doubling a letter is how crosswords make an abbreviation plural, so two Ns stand for more than one national.
P is the physics symbol for power, the one printed on plugs and bulbs.

explanation.surface: Somebody arranging a national championship while the real power quietly ascends.
explanation.walkthrough: A down entry runs top to bottom, so anything heading for heaven is climbing against it and the whole assembly has to be read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: A planner is the one who draws up the plan, so the definition names the person by the job they do.

clue.text: Criminal activity in team work

parts.note: The preposition is taken at face value, two letters as they stand.
A side is a team in British sport — the first team is the first side.
A job is a piece of work.

explanation.surface: Something shady going on within the team at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In team work' reads as one phrase about co-operation and is three separate pieces laid end to end, with 'in' meaning nothing beyond its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An inside job is a crime committed by someone within the organisation robbed, so it is one particular kind of criminal activity.

clue.text: Swedish tenor Björling accepting old incomplete birthright citizenship

indicators.note: Accepting something is taking it in, so the name closes around the letters that follow.

parts.note: Jussi Björling was Sweden's great operatic tenor, and it is his first name that does the work here.
'Old' turns up without its last letter.

explanation.surface: A famous Swedish tenor taking on an unfinished old song about where you were born.
explanation.walkthrough: Jus soli is Latin for right of the soil, and it is argued against jus sanguinis, right of blood, whenever countries fall out over who counts as a citizen.
explanation.definitionFit: Jus soli is the rule that being born on a country's soil makes you its citizen, which is birthright citizenship exactly.

clue.text: A mixture of sad and humane but not embarrassed

indicators.note: A mixture is what you get when things are stirred together and lose the order they arrived in.

parts.note: Three of the nine letters, going in as they stand.
The other six letters, which with the first three make exactly the enumeration.

explanation.surface: Someone both miserable and kind, and not the least bit awkward about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The two fodder words are a pair of character traits, which is why they read as description rather than as nine letters waiting to be stirred.
explanation.definitionFit: Unashamed means feeling no shame about something, so 'not embarrassed' catches it with the negative spelled out.

clue.text: Instrument's initial temperature increases which is welcome

indicators.note: 'Initial' points at the very first letter of the instrument's name, the only one that changes.

parts.note: The instrument is a cello, and only its first letter is touched.
C is the abbreviation for cold and H for hot, so raising the temperature swaps one for the other.

explanation.surface: An instrument's opening note warming up as the room does.
explanation.walkthrough: Both letters here are temperature abbreviations, C for cold and H for hot, which is what allows a rise in temperature to edit a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A hello is the greeting you give someone arriving, which is what 'welcome' names when it is used as a noun.

clue.text: TV channel doesn't show very popular dance music

indicators.note: What a channel doesn't show is not on screen, so the word named after it is not among the letters.

parts.note: The TV channel is Discovery, the documentary station.
These four letters are the ones taken out of the channel's name.

explanation.surface: A television channel refusing to broadcast some very popular dance music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very popular dance music' reads as one phrase, and the split comes a word earlier than it looks: 'very' belongs to the channel, not to the music.
explanation.definitionFit: Disco is the four-to-the-floor dance music that filled clubs in the seventies, so 'popular dance music' names the genre.

clue.text: Opera stars covering Bob Marley?

indicators.note: To cover something is to lie over it and keep it out of sight, so the letters are concealed by the words carrying them.

parts.note: Five consecutive letters straddle the join between these two words, starting three letters in.

explanation.surface: Opera singers having a go at Bob Marley's back catalogue.
explanation.walkthrough: Covering is what one band does to another band's song, which is the surface joke; the question mark admits that one man stands for a whole faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Marley was the most famous Rastafari of all, so he defines the answer by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Right around fireplace is a butterfly

indicators.note: Going around something means enclosing it, so the short piece opens up and the other lands inside.

parts.note: Rt is the abbreviation used in titles such as Rt Hon, the Right Honourable.
An ingle is an old word for a fireplace, the one still standing in 'inglenook'.

explanation.surface: Something turning about the hearth turns out to be a butterfly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks like the single R that crosswords use constantly for compass points and politics, and here it is the two-letter Rt of Rt Hon instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringlet is a dark brown European butterfly named for the small eye-rings on its wings, so the definition is by example.

clue.text: Inferior school shut

parts.note: Sch is the standard abbreviation for school, the one on signs and timetables.
To lock a door is to shut it fast.

explanation.surface: A failing school closing its gates for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inferior school shut' carries no instruction word at all, so the join between definition and wordplay has to be found by counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Schlock is cheap trashy stuff, and the word doubles as an adjective — a schlock film is an inferior one.

clue.text: Anarchic contra not pro FBI's measure of green policy

indicators.note: Anarchy is the absence of any order at all, so the letters beside it have none either.

parts.note: Fifteen letters, exactly the enumeration, going into the mix as they stand.

explanation.surface: Anarchists lining up against the FBI rather than for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contra not pro' says the same thing twice over, which is what makes it read as political sloganeering rather than as a heap of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbon footprint is the tonnage of greenhouse gas an activity causes, which is the number green policy is measured against.
